cue: How do you say time will make it hurt less?

es.meaning: Pain and difficulty fade with time.
es.example: Ahora parece imposible, pero el tiempo lo cura todo.
es.exampleTranslation: It feels impossible now, but time heals everything.

it.text: Il tempo guarisce tutte le ferite
it.meaning: Pain and difficulty fade with time.
it.example: Adesso sembra impossibile, ma il tempo guarisce tutte le ferite.
it.exampleTranslation: It feels impossible now, but time heals all wounds.

bridge.note: Same consolation, and Italian says what is being healed. Spanish keeps it abstract — todo, everything, whatever it was — while Italian names the wounds, ferite, and so quietly narrows the promise: time is good for injuries, not for every kind of trouble. The Spanish also carries a piece of grammar that has no Italian equivalent: el tiempo LO cura todo, with a pronoun that duplicates the todo coming after it. Nothing is missing if you remove it, and no Spanish speaker would.

interference.es_to_it: Italian does not double the object. 'Il tempo lo guarisce tutto' is wrong — there is no Italian counterpart to the Spanish redundant lo, and the fixed form names the wounds instead of gesturing at everything.
interference.it_to_es: Spanish needs the lo. 'El tiempo cura todo' is heard and is the weaker form; the proverb as fixed is 'el tiempo LO cura todo'. And Spanish does not name the wounds — 'el tiempo cura todas las heridas' exists as a calque but is not the traditional refrán.
